title: From printing matrix to edition and workshop exchange
question: Which sources identify the work, an individual impression, and the roles of its makers, and which evidence supports an exchange of printmaking practice between workshops?
summary: This pilot traces Kenojuak Ashevak’s 1962 stonecut The Arrival of the Sun through a cooperative catalogue, collection records, a film and the artist’s Inuktitut comments. It also tests one workshop-level claim about Japanese woodblock tools and Kinngait stonecut printing against evidence from before and after the exchange.
inputs: Work title, translated titles, maker and workshop aliases, and a broad date window
Impression accession, edition or proof notation, or matrix identifier
Contemporary catalogue or colophon and an independent holding institution, maker interview, or archive finding aid
Proposed source and recipient workshops, contact window, and a specific tool, operation, material, or division of work

steps.title: Find the work in the edition record
steps.action: Search the producer’s catalogue index by workshop and year. Search title variants, maker names, and item numbers in the original scans. If the PDF has no text layer, render or OCR the pages and check the image against any transcription. Record the image, catalogue number, medium, named roles, and separately any issue, exhibition, and production dates. Search the dataset and leads by the same titles and aliases.
steps.result: Searches for Kinngait and Cape Dorset with Kenojuak and both English and French titles found the cooperative’s scanned catalogue. PDF page 33 shows no. 69-62, The Arrival of the Sun / Retour du soleil, with Kenojuak as the named artist, the stonecut designation, and a ring of birds around the central sun. The distributor indexes the scan as 1962, while its front matter on PDF page 3 refers to graphics approved for 1963. The work date 1962 is independently recorded by the National Gallery of Canada. Treat the annual catalogue label, the work date, and publication or exhibition as separate fields. Dataset searches for Kinngait, Cape Dorset, Japanese printmaking, and the work title located the existing community practice record and its museum source.

steps.title: Distinguish edition, impression, proof and matrix
steps.action: Find the object at a holding institution by title, accession number and edition notation. Compare design and technique with the producer’s record, then search the exact title with block, plate, or stoneblock to identify a matrix. For a claim that two records concern the same sheet, require an accession or verifiable custody trail with a unique sheet mark, defect, or other identifying feature. Record measurements with their stated basis and flag unexplained differences.
steps.result: National Gallery accession 38038 records a black-and-yellow stonecut on japan paper gifted by the cooperative in 1995. The archived University of Lethbridge collection page for 1988.164 identifies a numbered impression 40/50. Matching title, artist, date, medium, and composition identify the catalogued work; neither the catalogue number 69-62 nor the denominator 50 identifies an individual sheet. The National Gallery’s 2000–01 annual report says the collection holds both the print and the stoneblock featured in the film, but gives no block accession there. No block accession or independent sheet-to-block comparison was found in the public title and accession searches. The published dimensions differ between the catalogue and the collection records, which do not consistently specify what was measured. The First Arts lot 20 sheet is an uninscribed, unnumbered proof reported to have belonged to Terry Ryan. The auction description itself calls its proposed identity with the filmed impression speculative. The film and lot 20 show the same work without establishing that the film shows that sheet.

steps.title: Trace what each participant did
steps.action: Transcribe credited names and roles from the original catalogue or the impression’s margins, retaining name and script variants. Search the work title and names in the workshop archive, film or audio finding aid, and maker interviews. Record whether each source names a role, shows a particular task, or repeats somebody else’s attribution. Compare recorded speech against any narrator or subtitles and document the translation used.
steps.result: The catalogue credits Kenojuak. The National Film Board film shows her examining a newly pulled impression. Rhoda Kayakjuak’s translation of the Inuktitut dialogue records Kenojuak pointing out an omitted eye when Terry Ryan asks about the print. The English narration substitutes a story about the source of her inspiration. This supports her role in designing and evaluating the print; the dialogue alone cannot show how the workshop acted on her feedback. Dorset Fine Arts captions a photo as Lukta Qiatsuq cutting this block. First Arts attributes cutting to Iyola Kingwatsiak and printing to Lukta Qiatsuk, interpreting the filmed sequence. The sources leave exclusive cutting credit unresolved and their claims cannot identify who pulled accession 38038. For the film sequence the pilot used the published frame and retranslated dialogue; repeated accounts of that same dialogue do not add a second witness.

steps.title: Test a named operation at both workshops
steps.action: Define one operation and its source and recipient separately. Search the partners’ names with the tool’s local and foreign names, date, and contact route. Find a donor-side object or account demonstrating the operation and an independently recorded recipient-side object, testimony, or work scene showing local adoption or adaptation. Require a dated common actor, shipment, training, or other bridge. Distinguish the primary items from the modern publication that brings them together.
steps.result: Searches combined Hiratsuka, Houston, Cape Dorset, and baren. The source side is Un’ichi Hiratsuka’s Japanese woodblock practice, specifically rubbing the back of the sheet for ink transfer. In a translated passage from his own 1962 account, Hiratsuka describes rubbing the paper between ink applications. Ikeda and Tiampo’s catalogue draft identifies the rubbing pad as a baren and describes Houston learning to make one. The draft cites a dated 3 November 1958 Houston note in the Alastair Grant Collection. The CMH exhibit inventory records Japanese prints transported to Cape Dorset by Houston on his return in 1959. On the recipient side, the inventory lists locally made tools used by Inuit printmakers, including a sealskin baren. The draft identifies it as CMC IV-C-3558, distinguishes its covering from Japanese bamboo leaf, reproduces contemporary NFB publicity photo PA-94469 showing Kananginak Pootoogook rubbing the paper with a baren, and reports his separate 2009 interview (interpreted by Jimmy Manning) recalling the distinctive Japanese tools. The draft and exhibit inventory share a curatorial lineage; the artist’s account, photographed task, and surviving tool are separate underlying evidence. Together they support adaptation of the rubbing tool at the Kinngait workshop. The photo could be posed and does not identify its baren as IV-C-3558. Hiratsuka’s original-language article and the Houston note were not inspected directly.

steps.title: Run a chronology and scope control
steps.action: Search for a dated pre-contact example of the claimed recipient operation, and for a post-contact case in which an available tool or image could be mistaken for a documented use. Compare the feature that actually travelled with recipient materials and production roles. For an independent check, search a physical object register or conservation report by identifier and a maker or photographer archive by date and participant.
steps.result: CMH’s object record places Niviaksiak’s Three Caribous stonecut, UN CD 1957/58-003 EXPE, in 1957. This predates Houston’s November 1958 departure and rules out that trip as the origin of Kinngait stonecut printing. The 1962 catalogue calls The Arrival of the Sun a stonecut and accession 38038 describes its paper as japan paper. Neither establishes which baren touched that sheet, its paper supplier, nor adoption of a complete Japanese workflow. The Kinngait evidence here includes several hands in production and does not establish Hiratsuka’s single-artist model there. The collected CMH block of 1960 is another work, Talluliyuk, Sea Goddess, as identified in the draft’s Fig. 27 (CMC IV-C-3559). For independent confirmation of the Arrival matrix, seek a block accession through the National Gallery’s collection documentation and compare the relief in reverse with the printed image; for a specific impression, look instead for an annotated proof, print-shop ledger, paper analysis or unique sheet feature tied to its accession.

decision: Accept the work-level match to 69-62 and Kenojuak’s role in designing and evaluating the impression shown. Accept workshop-level adaptation of a Japanese-style rubbing pad through Houston’s 1958–59 exchange. The film sheet’s identity and exclusive cutting credit remain unresolved. The earliest local stonecut in this test predates the exchange. The existing Kinngait practice record already describes the experiments and the later exchange, so retain this additional evidence in the workflow without creating an edition as a discovery or a workshop graph edge.
reject_if: A shared title, image, work number, or edition denominator alone is offered as proof that two records document one sheet. Reject a claimed origin if the recipient already used the operation before the proposed contact, and leave an adoption claim unresolved if the bridge or the recipient’s use evidence is absent.
stop_when: For a work join, stop when an original catalogue and an independently documented artifact agree on distinctive identifiers. For a sheet join or an individual role, stop only at an identifying object or primary workshop record, or record the missing identifier and leave the claim unresolved after checking the relevant public catalogues and archives. Admit a workshop exchange only at the scope where the source practice, dated bridge, and recipient use all converge.
next: Open the Povungnituk section of the same cooperative catalogue, PDF pp. 35–37. Start with Stuart Williams’s signed survey of the 1961 experiments and Victor Tinkl’s advisory role in 1962, then compare the item image under Qumalu, Qumaluk and the French title. Use Avataq’s historical catalogue archive and the Agnes Etherington Art Centre’s Puvirnituq holdings to seek the recipient impression and workshop documentation. The shared release establishes a publishing relationship and gives a starting point for testing any claimed transfer of printing practice.
